config.title: Type async hooks with generic result and error

intro.title: Type async hooks with generic result and error
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a custom React hook that handles asynchronous operations, such as fetching data from an API, with proper TypeScript typing. You'll learn to use TypeScript generics to create a flexible hook that can return different data types and error types, making your code reusable and type-safe. The main technologies involved are React hooks (useState, useEffect), async/await for handling promises, and TypeScript generics for defining dynamic types. By the end, you'll have a typed async hook that manages loading states, results, and errors, improving your app's reliability and developer experience.
intro.usecase: In modern web applications, async hooks with typed results and errors are essential for handling data fetching in components like dashboards, admin panels, and data tables. For example, when building a user management dashboard, developers need to fetch user lists, update permissions, or delete accounts—each operation requiring specific result types and error handling. By properly typing these async hooks, you ensure that components consuming the data (like user tables or permission modals) receive correctly structured responses and can display appropriate loading states, success messages, or error notifications. This pattern prevents runtime errors and improves developer experience with autocomplete and type checking across complex data flows.

objectives: Implement a custom hook that manages asynchronous data fetching in TypeScript.
Apply generic type parameters to define the shape of result and error data in the hook.
Initialize state variables to track loading status, fetched results, and potential errors.
Construct an async function within the hook to perform the data fetching operation.
Manipulate state updates to reflect loading, success, and error states during the fetch lifecycle.
Integrate the typed async hook into a React component to display fetched data or error messages.
Configure the hook to accept and use a generic fetch function as a dependency.

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from 'react'.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing React and a hook
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library and useState hook are imported and available for use.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: import both React and useState from the 'react' package.

steps.title: Create a generic AsyncResult type
steps.instruction: Create a generic TypeScript type named AsyncResult<T> with three properties: loading (boolean), data (T | null), and error (string | null).
steps.hint: Define a type using the 'type' keyword with a generic parameter <T>. Inside curly braces, list the properties with their types.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';
// Create a generic AsyncResult type here
steps.expectedOutcome: A reusable generic type that can represent the three states of an async operation: loading, success (with data), and error.
successCriteria: The AsyncResult<T> type is defined with the correct generic parameter and three typed properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your type has all three properties: loading (boolean), data (T | null), and error (string | null).
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the syntax. You need to define a type named AsyncResult<T> with the three required properties.

steps.title: Create the useAsync hook function
steps.instruction: Create a function named useAsync that accepts a generic type parameter T and returns AsyncResult<T>. Use a function declaration or arrow function.
steps.hint: Define a function that takes no arguments and returns an AsyncResult object. You can use the generic type parameter T in the function signature.
steps.expectedOutcome: A useAsync function is defined with proper TypeScript typing, ready to be implemented in later steps.
successCriteria: The useAsync function is created, accepts a generic type parameter T, and returns AsyncResult<T>.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the function returns AsyncResult<T> and accepts the generic type parameter T.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function is missing or doesn't match the required signature. It should accept a generic type parameter T and return AsyncResult<T>.

steps.title: Initialize state with AsyncResult type
steps.instruction: Inside your useAsync hook, initialize a state variable using useState with the AsyncResult<T> type. Set the initial state to an object with status 'idle', data as null, and error as null.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook with explicit typing: useState<AsyncResult<T>>({ status: 'idle', data: null, error: null })
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: typed state initialization
const [user, setUser] = useState<{ name: string; age: number }>({ name: '', age: 0 });
steps.expectedOutcome: The useAsync hook will have a properly typed state variable initialized with the default async state values.
successCriteria: State is initialized using useState with AsyncResult<T> type and default values { status: 'idle', data: null, error: null }
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using the AsyncResult<T> type and setting all three properties: status, data, and error.
steps.feedbackWrong: use useState with the AsyncResult<T> type and provide the initial state object.

steps.title: Define the async operation handler
steps.instruction: Inside the useAsync function, define an async function named 'execute' that takes a parameter 'asyncFn' (a function returning a Promise of type T) and returns a Promise of type T. This function should set loading state, call asyncFn, handle the result or error, and update state accordingly.
steps.hint: Remember to use the setState function from useState to update the state with the appropriate AsyncResult values (loading, data, error).
steps.expectedOutcome: The useAsync hook now contains an 'execute' function that properly handles async operations with loading, success, and error states.
successCriteria: An async 'execute' function is defined inside useAsync that takes an asyncFn parameter, sets loading state, calls asyncFn, and updates state with result or error.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your execute function is async, takes an asyncFn parameter, properly sets loading state, and updates state with both success and error results.
steps.feedbackWrong: The execute function is missing or incomplete. It should be an async function that handles the complete async operation lifecycle.

steps.title: Return the state and handler from hook
steps.instruction: Inside the useAsync hook, return an object containing the current async state and the handler function.
steps.hint: The return statement should be the last line of your hook function. Return an object with properties for the state and handler.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useAsync hook now returns an object with typed state and handler, making them available to components that use this hook.
successCriteria: The hook returns an object containing the async state and the handler function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're returning an object with both the state and handler function from your hook.
steps.feedbackWrong: The hook isn't returning the expected values. Check that you're returning an object containing both the async state and the handler function.

steps.title: Create a component to use the hook
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named DemoComponent that will use the useAsync hook. The component should return a simple wrapper div element.
steps.hint: Define a component function that returns a JSX div element. You'll use the hook inside this component in later steps.
steps.expectedOutcome: A DemoComponent function is created that returns a JSX div element.
successCriteria: DemoComponent is defined as a functional component and returns a JSX div element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you've defined a function named DemoComponent that returns a JSX div element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component wasn't created correctly. Create a functional component named DemoComponent that returns a JSX div element.

steps.title: Use the hook with specific data type
steps.instruction: Inside your DemoComponent, call the useAsync hook with a concrete type parameter (e.g., string[]) and destructure the returned state and handler.
steps.hint: Call the hook like useAsync<string[]>() and destructure the result into variables like result and execute.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: calling a typed hook
const { data, loading } = useFetch<string[]>();
steps.expectedOutcome: The DemoComponent should call useAsync with a specific type (like string[]) and destructure the returned object.
successCriteria: useAsync is called with a concrete type parameter and its return value is destructured.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure to both specify the type parameter and destructure the hook's return value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The hook call or destructuring is missing. Check that you're calling useAsync<string[]>() and destructuring the result.

steps.title: Add UI to display async state
steps.instruction: Inside your DemoComponent, add conditional JSX rendering that shows different UI based on the async state: display a loading message when loading is true, an error message when error exists, and the data when it's available.
steps.hint: You can use the destructured result, loading, and error values from useAsync. Use conditional rendering with logical AND (&&) or ternary operators to show appropriate UI for each state.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will display appropriate UI for loading, error, and data states when you implement the async operation.
successCriteria: The DemoComponent returns JSX with conditional rendering for loading, error, and data states using the destructured values from useAsync.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some conditional rendering, but make sure you handle all three states: loading, error, and data.
steps.feedbackWrong: The conditional rendering isn't implemented correctly. Check that you're using the destructured values (result, loading, error) from useAsync and showing appropriate UI for each state.

steps.title: Add button to trigger async operation
steps.instruction: Inside the DemoComponent's return statement, add a button element with an onClick handler that calls the async operation function you destructured from useAsync.
steps.hint: Place the button inside the div, after any existing content. Use onClick={asyncOperation} where asyncOperation is the handler you destructured.
steps.expectedOutcome: The DemoComponent will have a button that, when clicked, triggers the async operation defined in the useAsync hook.
successCriteria: A button element with onClick={asyncOperation} is added inside the DemoComponent's return statement.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a button, but make sure the onClick handler correctly calls the async operation function from useAsync.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button is missing or the onClick handler is not correctly wired to the async operation function.
